title: Current and saved context
intro: Current context is supplied now. Saved memory is information retained for later use. A stored record is not automatically visible to the model.
takeaway: Persistence and visibility are separate: storage retains a record; retrieval supplies it to a later invocation.

beats.text: The model receives its current input. This is the context it can use now.
Other records exist in a memory store. Their presence does not include them.
The application must retrieve a record. Then it can include it in a new input.
Supply that record to the next call. The saved copy stays in the store.

title: Choose the memory scope
intro: Thread-scoped state belongs to a conversation. A separate store can hold records used across conversations. Either may use persistent storage.
takeaway: Short-term describes scope, not necessarily RAM. The backend determines what survives process restarts.

beats.text: Thread state belongs to one conversation. It can include saved progress.
A shared store has a wider scope. Use namespaces and keys for its records.
A new session reads the relevant scope. It should not mix unrelated histories.
Scope and durability are different choices. Check what the backend actually retains.

title: Save a useful record
intro: Before retaining a fact, decide whether it is useful, supported and appropriate for later use. Include provenance and applicability such as repository revision.
takeaway: Memory writes need policy. Repeatedly storing an unsupported inference can make later answers consistently wrong.

beats.text: The session finds the test command. It proposes retaining that information.
Check its source and intended scope. A guess should not become a settled fact.
Save the command with its revision. Future readers can check applicability.
Retain only what the policy allows. More stored notes are not always better.

title: Check applicability
intro: A new checkout uses pnpm test at revision r2. Retrieval returns an older r1 note. Application-side checks reject the stale command.
takeaway: Relevant does not mean current. Revision validation is deliberately implemented here, not an automatic feature of every memory store.

beats.text: A saved note says npm test at r1. The checkout now uses revision r2.
Retrieval returns the relevant old note. Compare its revision with the checkout.
Reject the stale command for this task. Read the current repository instructions.
Supply pnpm test from revision r2. The model gets applicable evidence.

title: Correct outdated memory
intro: When authoritative instructions change, update or supersede retained notes according to the memory policy. Preserve enough history to explain the correction.
takeaway: Memory needs maintenance and access controls. Removing stale applicability is different from pretending the old note was never valid.

beats.text: The authoritative command changed at r2. The stored r1 note is now outdated.
Mark the old record as superseded. Keep its earlier revision explicit.
Store the current command and source. The new record applies to r2.
Later retrieval selects a matching version. Still validate it against the current task.
